title: Va'etchanan: the Shema whole (Deuteronomy 6:4–9)
hookLine: love God with all your heart, soul and might
tomorrow: Va'etchanan: at home and on the way (Deuteronomy 6:7)

lines: SIX WORDS, A HAND OVER THE EYES.
cards: Many Jewish children learn the Shema before they can read: six Hebrew words, said with a hand over the eyes.

It's said at bedtime, in the morning service and the evening service, and for many centuries it has been the words Jews hoped to say at the very end of life. The first line is often said on its own, like a motto.
In the Torah it isn't on its own at all. It sits in Moses' farewell, in the sixth chapter of Deuteronomy, and the very next word opens a paragraph.

teach.b: First the line, in the old Jewish translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."

Then, without a pause in the text: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The first Hebrew word of that second verse is today's word. V'ahavta.
And thou shalt love. It names the whole paragraph that Jews say right after the Shema. And it raises a question the rabbis took seriously: can love be commanded?
The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, answers by taking the three phrases one at a time.
With all thy heart: the Hebrew spells heart here with a doubled letter, levavcha, and the Mishnah hears two hearts, so love God with both your inclinations, the good one and the selfish one.
Your whole messy self, not just your best moods. With all thy soul: even if your life is taken.

The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying under Roman torture, said the Shema and drew out the final word, one, until his breath ended. With all thy might: the Mishnah reads it as with all your money, your resources.
And it adds one more: for whatever measure is measured out to you, good or bad, give thanks. So the command isn't to feel warm.

teach.h: BOTH HEARTS, YOUR LIFE, YOUR MIGHT.
teach.b: It's to bring everything, the good impulses and the bad, your life, your wallet, your luck, into one direction.
The paragraph that follows tells how: these words on your heart, taught to your children, on your doorposts.

how: Jews recite the Shema and the V'ahavta paragraph in the morning and evening services and at bedtime, many covering their eyes for the first line; the passage is also written inside the mezuzah and tefillin.

o: and thou shalt hear: the Shema's first word
and thou shalt love: the verse after the Shema
and thou shalt teach: the line on doorposts

games.q: inside the paragraph — tap the pairs.
p: even if your life is taken

s: the Shema is a standalone line with nothing after it
it's Deuteronomy 6:4, and v'ahavta follows straight on in 6:5.
the Mishnah reads with all thy might as with all your money
the Mishnah says to give thanks only for the good
for whatever measure is measured out to you, good or bad.

games.q: the verse commands love with all thy heart. the Hebrew spells heart with a doubled letter. what does the Mishnah make of it?
o: love God only with your best self.
love God with both inclinations, the good and the selfish.
games.why: levavcha, two hearts: love God with the good inclination and the selfish one too.

practice: If you pray, cover your eyes and say the first line, Shema Yisrael, in Hebrew or English, then the next verse slowly, a breath between each phrase.
If you don't, hold the three phrases as questions: what would all your heart include, what do you give your life to, and where does your might, your money and your time, actually go?

wordCard.voice: V'ahavta. And thou shalt love. The verse after the Shema, and the name of the paragraph said with it, morning and night.

orig.note: Hebrew: and thou shalt love. the first word of Deuteronomy 6:5, naming the paragraph after the Shema.

carryVoice: Your line: with all your heart. The messy parts count too. That's day four hundred eighty-nine.
